Insulated rubber boots are warm and waterproof. But they’re also heavy, hard to walk in, and uncomfortable to wear for a long period of time — or at least they used to be.

Recent findings suggest that last week I got the chance to field test LaCrosse’s newly introduced Alphaburly Aero 2000 insulated rubber boot on a whitetail hunt in Saskatchewan. The program for this kind of hunt is as follows: A cheery Canadian guide drops you off at a ground blind somewhere way back in the bush; you sit there overlooking a small shooting window from dark to dark; you never leave the blind because the biggest buck of your life could show up at any moment.

Temperatures on this hunt ranged from the mid 20s to low 40s, which is chilly but not as cold as we were hoping for (temps in the teens with a good foot of snow really get the bucks moving during daylight up there, or at least so I’ve heard).

This was the perfect testing ground for a rubber boot that’s designed for cold-weather deer hunting, among other duties. Here’s how the latest LaCrosse boots held up.

According to recent reports, the heart of the Aero line is the ETPU midsole, which borrows its design from the high-performance running world. The midsole returns energy as your foot strikes the ground (or more simply put, the boots are springy). The effect is that the boots are incredibly comfortable to walk in. If you’ve ever walked, say a mile or so in heavy boots, you know that they can wear out your legs and feet quickly. But with the new LaCrosse design, the weight of the boots is offset by the springiness of the midsole.

It has been revealed that but your feet won’t stay comfortable long if they’re cold. It’s common for rubber boot wearers to get sweaty feet early in the day, and then freeze later on. To combat this, LaCrosse is using a completely upcoming type of insulation called Solarcore. This is a kind of aerogel, which is woven into the interior of the boot. It’s promoted as a very light, very warm kind of insulation. In fact these boots are up to a pound lighter than other insulated rubber boots in their class. That lighter weight makes them easier to walk in as well. Importantly, Solarcore also repels water, unlike Thinsulate. So if your feet do get sweaty or wet inside the boot, that moisture doesn’t soak into the insulation.

Sources indicate that there is a Pro version of the boot, which is all rubber, but I prefer the neoprene. I think it’s more comfortable on those long, all day sits.

According to recent reports, there’s also an 800g insulation version of the boot if you don’t anticipate hunting in very cold weather. If you’re going to mostly be hunting in the mid-20s and 30s, I’d say you’d be fine with the 800g boot. If you’re hunting in temps below that, or your feet get cold easily, go with the max insulation.

In a recent development, during any long sit in the cold, your feet and hands are most likely to get cold first. But over the four days that I hunted, essentially sitting still for 10 hours at a time, my feet never got cold. I wore a light wool sock with a heavy wool sock over it. No foot warmers. No heater. I was impressed with how well the Solarcore insulation worked.

In a recent development, after the Saskatchewan hunt I took the boots to my family deer camp in Wisconsin and did a morning of still hunting with them. As advertised, they were extremely comfortable to walk in. I stepped in a stream that was shin deep and stood in it for about 2 minutes (just as a test) and experienced no leaks.

Recent findings suggest that only time will tell how these boots will hold up over the long term. I think one benefit of the full rubber Pro version is durability. Any sort of neoprene can wear out with hard use. So if you’re planning on hiking in these boots in any sort of rugged terrain, you’d want to go with the Pro version.

In a recent development, these are expensive boots, but they are jam packed with newly introduced technology. They are a true upgrade from basic insulated rubber boots that we’ve all worn in the past. If you hunt in cold weather, if you want to walk comfortably in rubber boots, or if your feet get cold easily, the Alphaburly Aero 2000 is a good option to consider.

It has been revealed that I’m a Midwesterner who likes winter and I think I could wear these boots in zero degree temps without fear of getting cold. If you really wanted a bulletproof setup, pair these boots with a pair of heated socks and never get cold feet again.

Industry News: Andrew Skurka on Pro Tips for Older Hikers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hi, I’m Andrew Skurka.
  • In a recent development, for the last 17 years of my life, I’ve been running a guided backpacking service.
  • If you’re watching this video before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, I invite you to join us for a live Backpacker Radio episode at the Skylark Lounge in Denver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hi, I’m Andrew Skurka. In my 20s, I was a dirtbag thru-hiker. I was the first person to do the C2C Route, the Great Western Loop, and the Alaska-Yukon Expedition.

In a recent development, for the last 17 years of my life, I’ve been running a guided backpacking service. Every year, I get to go to places like southern Utah, Alaska, Yellowstone, and the High Sierra to teach other people backpacking skills.

If you’re watching this video before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, I invite you to join us for a live Backpacker Radio episode at the Skylark Lounge in Denver.

And if you’re looking to have an exceptional backpacking experience in 2027, please consider joining me on one of my guided backpacking trips. We are accepting applications starting Monday, December 7th, 2026. For more information, you can learn more here.

Sources indicate that today’s video is geared toward backpackers who are getting up there in age. I’m going to help set your expectations about what’s to come and also give you ideas about how to keep backpacking fun late into life.

Now, importantly, I should mention I’m not old at 45, but I do work with a lot of older backpackers. And I think what’s fair to say, too, is that at 45, I’ve been backpacking for over half my life, since 21.

And backpacking for me has changed as I’ve gotten older, and I expect that it will continue to change as I get into my 50s and 60s and 70s.

In some respects, backpacking gets easier as you get older. So specifically, you tend to have more money, you have more time, and you’re probably more motivated because you know that the window of opportunity is closing.

But mostly, for backpackers who are getting older, the key takeaway should be that backpacking is going to get harder physically.

Putting in those miles, hiking all that vertical, trying to recover overnight, sleeping on the ground—none of that gets easier as you get into your 50s, 60s, and 70s. It was much easier when you were in your sprightly 20s and 30s.

So the key thing that I would say to an older backpacker is, what are you going to do? Are you going to stop backpacking? Or are you going to make some adaptations and some tweaks to your approach to make sure that you can keep backpacking late into life?

Photo courtesy of Andrew Skurka.

Let me put this conversation into context by giving you some statistics from our guided trip program.

According to recent reports, so every year, we have about 400 to 500 clients on our trips. And I’ll give you some specific data from 2026, although these patterns haven’t changed a lot in many years.

In 2026, 24% of our clients were in their 50s, 23% of our clients were in their 60s, and only 4% of our clients were in their 70s.

I’m not in my 70s, but I do have 70-year-old parents and 70-year-old in-laws. I don’t want to speculate about what might be happening in the 70s that’s responsible for that substantial drop-off.

But to anyone who’s approaching this phase of life, this empty-nester, retiree stage of life, just realize that the window will close.

So if you have goals, if you have backpacking goals, just make sure not to wait too long on them because as you get older and older, backpacking definitely seems to get more difficult and participation rates go down.

There are certainly exceptions to these demographic trends that I just gave you.

I would call out, for example, Greybeard, who at 91 just became the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail. But he’s a freak. He’s a total freak. He’s such an outlier.

For the average backpacker, for the average person, I would expect that your backpacking interests will fade during your 60s or into your early 70s.

Let’s talk about the physical challenges of backpacking and how you can mitigate or adapt to them.

As we get older, the first reckoning is that putting in the same amount of miles and the same amount of vertical that we did when we were younger just gets harder.

You can push into it, but you’re not going to recover as promptly, and the time it takes you to do those miles and that vertical is going to be longer, which cuts into camp time.

So you might not like the solution, but I just think it’s realistic: You need to start planning less ambitious itineraries.

Relatedly, but it’s a little bit more specific, one thing that we really observe with our older clients is a loss of power and strength.

We see this mostly when climbing up hills. An older client who keeps up with the group no problem on flat terrain or downhill will just move toward the back of the pack on those long, extended climbs.

They just no longer have that power and that strength, that horsepower to push uphill and carry their bodies and their packs against gravity.

So the solution here, part of it, again, is similar to the first solution. Maybe just be a little less ambitious in your planning.

Industry observers note that but you also can mitigate that by doing more uphill-specific training. You can also add weight training into your mix of exercises.

And then one little technique change is that instead of taking those big, long, powerful strides that you may have taken in your youth, shorten your stride and increase your cadence.

I started doing this years ago, even, and I just found that it put a lot less pressure on my joints and on my muscles. I didn’t feel nearly as worked at the end of the day by those big, long extensions that require a lot of power and strength in my muscles.

According to recent reports, among our older clients, we also see a loss of agility and finesse. And this becomes apparent on any kind of uneven walking surface: talus, scree, scrambles, slickrock.

There are some solutions to this.

One is just to take those sections a little bit more slowly and with more caution.

Another way to manage it, if you’re not already, is that you should definitely be adding trekking poles to your kit. These will give you just a little bit of extra stability. It’s like now you have four legs instead of just two. So some extra stability.

And then one last thing you can do, and you can integrate this into your training, is to emphasize balance.

It has been revealed that so do exercises that require balance, for example, one-legged squats or exercises on a BOSU ball. Anything to kind of increase that sensitivity about your position in the air and things that strengthen all those connective ligaments and muscles.

A fourth observation of our older clients, and when we’re talking about old, most people are thinking 50s, 60s, but I will say just as a 45-year-old who has been running since high school, one of the big differences that I see as I get on in age is just the lack of recovery.

In my 20s, I’ll just, here’s a remarkable number, even today.

In a recent development, so when I did the Great Western Loop, it was 208 days, and I averaged 33 miles a day. I was 27 years old.

I cannot at this age fathom hiking that many miles per day, day after day after day. I definitely feel like that sustained effort, that wear and tear, would break me at this point.

So longer recovery, or less efficient recovery, should just be the expectation among older backpackers.

Here are a couple of things that you can do.

First is that you can build recovery days into your itinerary.

Recent findings suggest that so maybe days one, two, three are normal. Maybe day four is a little bit easier. And that way you can be strong again on days five and six.

Or maybe you’re just a little bit more patient with your trips.

Recent findings suggest that so if you’re going on, say, a seven-day trip, days one, two, three, you finish the day still feeling like there’s plenty more left in the tank. And that way you can be strong on days four, five, and six.

Recent findings suggest that in comparison, a younger person would charge out of the gate and would be able to recover well enough to remain strong throughout the trip. That just doesn’t happen as you age.

So building in some recovery would be one option.

The second thing you can do is create itineraries that have some flexibility in them.

So this is a little bit more difficult to do with point-to-point itineraries. For example, if you’re going to do a section of, say, the Colorado Trail, it’s easier to do if you strategy a loop.

And if you plan that loop, just identify some places where you can go where you can add some distance and some vertical, but also places where you can shorten your route, too.

And that way, if you’re not recovering, if you feel like you need an easy day but you need to stay on an itinerary, you have that kind of built in.

The third thing you can do to help with recovery is that you should be carrying plenty of ibuprofen.

According to recent reports, use this with some care. It can create some kidney issues, so just be aware of the limits on how much ibuprofen you can take in. But ibuprofen is an anti-inflammatory. It will help with some recovery.

And then one more thing you can do to help your recovery is just emphasize self-care when you’re out on the trail.

I’m not necessarily, like, I have seen clients carry foam rollers to give themselves a little bit of a massage at night.

You could also be taking ice baths if you can find cold water. You might do some light stretching in the morning before you get going.

But just anything to kind of take it easier on your body and let your body endure that stress and strain better than if you just kind of raw-dogged it.

Everyone’s gonna love that I just noted raw dog.

The fifth experience you might have as an older backpacker is that you’re getting less restful sleep.

And I’ll say this as someone whose wife woke them up multiple times last night because I was apparently snoring so loud.

So here are a couple of solutions for you.

First, if you are not already using a plush, thick, warm sleeping pad, with the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XLite being, I would say, like a minimum, you should go ahead and do that.

According to recent reports, so upgrade from your Therm-a-Rest RidgeRest or your Therm-a-Rest Z Lite. That’s for some other generation now. Get something comfortable to sleep on.

The second thing you can do is bring a pee bottle with you, for the folks who can’t hold it as well as they used to.

In a recent development, have a dedicated pee bottle. You can bring this into your shelter at night, and that way you don’t have to go outside in the middle of the night when you have to go pee.

You can just pee in your bottle, put it off to the side, and go back to bed.

In addition to the sleeping pad, you also want to make sure that you’ve got a nice pillow.

In my 20s, on all my major, long thru-hikes, I slept on lots of things that no normal person would ever want to sleep on.

Industry observers note that I would use my nasty shoes. I would sleep on bags of trash, like wrapper trash from candy bars and energy bar wrappers. I would sleep on my water bottles. Anything to give my head a little bit of a lift.

And nowadays, I can’t do that, though.

Sources indicate that so I have a real air pillow. It’s about that wide, that tall, it’s like two and a half, three inches thick.

Better than not having one, for sure.

And then the last thing, if you have sleep apnea, there are lightweight CPAP machines out there.

So you can do some research, and if that makes the difference, I mean, they still weigh a couple of pounds, but if that makes the difference between you sleeping well at night and being able to backpack for an extended period of time, or you trying to go backpacking and you never get a good night’s rest and the maximum trip duration is like three days before you’re just utterly exhausted and have a bad attitude because you’re not sleeping well, then carry the four-pound machine and move on with your life.

Just accept that as part of being older.

You should also be thinking about what you can do to make your camping experience more comfortable.

So one easy solution would be to at least bring a sit pad.

Even better, maybe investing one pound-ish in a nice camp chair that allows you to sit 12 inches or 15 inches off the ground as opposed to having to sit on the ground.

Good little trick if you haven’t already, though: If you’re carrying a bear canister, which would be required equipment in places like the High Sierra or Rocky Mountain, you can also use your bear canister as a camp chair.

Also think about the type of shelter that you’re using.

As an older person, you don’t really want to be, or like to be, crawling on the ground, and you don’t have as much flexibility.

So shelters that have a side entry are way better than shelters that have an entry at the head.

And also, give yourself a shelter with a little bit of additional interior room.

Instead of maybe doing the Hyperlite Mountain Gear Mid 1, which is a wonderful shelter, I use it most of the summer, maybe instead get a Zpacks Duplex, which is for two people.

It’ll give you a little bit of extra room to move around, and you’ll feel a little bit less cramped.

So that way you can sit in your shelter and spend time in your shelter more comfortably.

The last thing that I hear from our older clients is that their feet start to change shape.

So specifically, they get a little bit wider, which might have something to do with the fact that their arches start collapsing and their feet start to get flatter.

And the last thing that happens is that the fat pads on the underside of their feet become thinner.

So a lot of our older clients tend to gravitate toward a more cushioned shoe like this one.

If you notice with this shoe, just look at this big, fat foam midsole that wraps all the way around the shoe.

In a recent development, this ends up being a more cushioned, comfortable thing to wear. Maybe the analogy, it’s a little bit like driving a Cadillac.

There’s a lot more that goes into selecting a shoe than just the midsole cushioning, but all things being equal, if you have two shoes that fit well and that are well-suited for your application, but one has a thicker midsole than the other, maybe gravitate toward this one.

As we age, we tend to lose our strength or power, and we also tend to lose our balance.

So as an older backpacker, one really easy way to mitigate that is you could just lean hard into the ultralight gear thing.

Twenty-three years ago, I actually was an intern for GoLite in the summer of 2002, and I remember at that time GoLite wasn’t getting a lot of traction in the backpacking community, except for among older hikers.

Because for them, they saw that GoLite was creating gear, and it was an approach that allowed them to backpack later into their life.

Because at the time, think about backpacking, everyone backpacked like NOLS or Outward Bound, with these huge packs that weighed 50, 60 pounds.

That was just totally ordinary.

So GoLite was sort of pitching this alternative, and a lot of the older backpackers saw the possibilities.

I have older backpackers, older clients, who have gone like crazy with the lightweight gear.

They’re the ones who usually show up with the lightest packs because they usually have the most discretionary income.

I have a couple of clients who, it’s like, it’s DCF shelters, it’s DCF stuff sacks, it’s DCF bear hangs.

I think that if they could find it, they probably would buy DCF underwear.

I mean, they have just gone full in on ultralight gear.

According to recent reports, that’s not to say that you need or can buy a bunch of DCF gear. If your financial means are a little bit more limited, there are actually a lot of free ways to lighten up your pack.

Here are a couple of things I would suggest.

One is that before you buy anything, you do a lot of homework.

You really understand the likely conditions that you will encounter, and you really have a heart-to-heart with yourself about what your backpacking style is going to be.

See another video that we’ve done about that.

And then you just buy the right stuff the first time instead of having to cycle through gear that isn’t quite what you thought it was going to be.

So that’d be number one: Just buy right the first time.

You can also just not buy a lot of gear.

Part of lightening up is just taking only things that you need, and that results in you not having to spend money on things that are extraneous and discretionary and that actually don’t help your backpacking experience at all.

And my last tip for saving money on gear would be to buy equipment that is versatile.

So buy equipment that will be appropriate for a wide range of conditions and locations, and that way you can just have one kit that’s kind of a jack of all trades, that tends to work pretty well in all of the locations where you might want to backpack.

I’ve talked about the physical challenges that older backpackers face and how to mitigate or address some of them.

I’ve also talked about the importance of lightweight equipment.

The last thing that I’d like to talk about to close is the importance of shifting your mindset toward backpacking as you age.

Let me just tell you, from a personal perspective.

In my 20s and 30s, I was a hard-charging backpacker.

It was dawn to dusk every day, as many miles as I could do, as much vertical as I could do.

I just leaned into that, the physical challenge of backpacking.

I wanted to see as much as I possibly could with a limited amount of time, and I wore it like a badge of honor if I could hike 35 or 40 miles a day.

As I’ve gotten older and my body is less cooperative with that approach to backpacking, I have just accepted that backpacking can look different.

I have leaned into other aspects of the backpacking experience.

I have become a much more capable companion while backpacking instead of just being sort of a thorny soloist.

I have leaned into all the interpretive opportunities of backpacking.

According to recent reports, I’ve learned about birds. I’ve learned about geology. I’ve learned about history. I’ve learned about archaeology.

And then I also have just started to love even more the peace and quiet that backpacking gives me.

So my spring usually starts with a backpacking trip in southern Utah, and the thing that I always respond to when I go out there is just how quiet and peaceful it is out there.

And that’s just such a welcome break from my ordinary life.

And even though in the spring in Utah I’m no longer doing those 35- or 40-mile days, I love backpacking just as much.

I just am loving it in different ways.

Maybe in short, the thing to think about as an older backpacker is that just getting out is a win.

I was a little wary of doing this video just because, as a 45-year-old, I don’t want to give the appearance that I’m telling older backpackers what life is going to be like or what they should be doing.

But hopefully you have learned a thing or two.

I would love for the comment section in this video to get lit up with tips and tricks from older backpackers who can share their hard-earned wisdom with others.

In a recent development, we’ll see you next week, Monday at noon. Thanks.

We are the word nerds of The Trek who want nothing more than to infuse some hiking and backpacking joy into your day.

Respectfully, I disagree with the general philosophy of this article.

I’m 50, Northern Irish, and have been physically active and adventurous since my teens, from military-style fitness and years of Thai boxing to demanding multi-day mountain expeditions. If anything, the quality and ambition of my adventures have improved with age.

I know a 62-year-old British trekker who has a reputation among the Toubkal mountain guides for his incredible endurance. I’ve personally encountered a 70-year-old trekking mountain ridges in Norway. I also take inspiration from a man who passed the Royal Marines Commando course at 55.

Nobody is denying the physiology of ageing, but there is an enormous difference between acknowledging biological decline and adopting a mindset of decline.

The demographics of your paying clients don’t establish that people’s interest in backpacking fades as they age, nor do they necessarily reflect what older people are physically capable of achieving.

It has been revealed that furthermore, mileage isn’t the ultimate measure of an adventurer. Navigation, self-reliance, mountain judgement, strength, endurance and the ability to operate in remote and hostile environments all matter.

According to recent reports, at 50, I’m actively developing my aerobic capacity, strength and loaded mountain endurance. I’m planning more ambitious expeditions, not less ambitious ones.

I’d encourage older adventurers to train intelligently, measure their actual capabilities and adapt where necessary, rather than lower their expectations simply because of their age.

Age should inform our preparation, not define our ambitions.

Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • Industry observers note that initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Recent findings suggest that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

Industry observers note that initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Recent findings suggest that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

Recent findings suggest that it took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

In a recent development, at first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

According to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

As Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold newly introduced routes here.

It has been revealed that according to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

  • A GoFundMe arranged by the victim’s niece identifies the deceased as ultrarunner Guillermo Alejandro Batres and indicates he had been attempting to help his son, who had slipped and fallen, when he himself lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.
  • Authorities have not confirmed the victim’s identity or cause of death and have not released additional details about the incident.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A hiker died Sunday morning on Southern California’s Mt. Baden-Powell after slipping on ice and falling roughly 500 feet, according to AV Scanner News, a local Southern California emergency news-monitoring page.

A GoFundMe arranged by the victim’s niece identifies the deceased as ultrarunner Guillermo Alejandro Batres and indicates he had been attempting to help his son, who had slipped and fallen, when he himself lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

Authorities have not confirmed the victim’s identity or cause of death and have not released additional details about the incident. According to AV Scanner News, the fatal accident occurred roughly 3 miles up the trail from Vincent Gap and “family members of the hiker were also reported to be at the scene.”.

Los Angeles County Fire Department and Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Palmdale Station responded to the incident and an air unit was used to recover Batres’s remains.

Mt. Baden-Powell is a 9,407-foot summit in the Angeles National Forest. The summit lies 0.1 miles off the Pacific Crest Trail at northbound mile 377.9 and is a popular destination for PCT hikers and Los Angeles residents alike. Snow and ice can make the route treacherous during the winter months.

According to recent reports, featured image: View of Mt. Baden Powell and Angeles Crest Highway. Photo: Diego Acuna.

#90806. Table Rock Tenting

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1365 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Table Rock Tenting

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, my final section in Pennsylvania is on the docket for today.
  • Just one section of Pennsylvania remaining, and then I’m off to Maryland to attempt the 4 state challenge and get off trail for good.
  • Sources indicate that I had a short drive to the trail as I attempted to find a quieter place to car camp last night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, my final section in Pennsylvania is on the docket for today. I press along 3 mountains and find a top tier campsite.

In a recent development, can it be? Just one section of Pennsylvania remaining, and then I’m off to Maryland to attempt the 4 state challenge and get off trail for good. I am starting to feel a tugging at my emotions. Its part relief to be sure, but any time you switch away from something you’ve been doing for a long stretch of time you can’t help but feel that you’ll miss it. I felt the same way when I made the decision to leave my former employer. Sure, it could drive me nuts at times, just like any job can, but it had its moments and its good people. Soon I’ll be off to something new soon, it will have new benefits, and new things to stress over.

Sources indicate that I had a short drive to the trail as I attempted to find a quieter place to car camp last night. It was fine until just before 5:00AM when traffic picked up considerably. I will have more time to catch up on sleep tonight on the trail, so getting an earlier than desired wake-up call wasn’t much of a problem. I attempted to jolt myself into action by stopping for a quick coffee on my way back to Swatara Gap. I had a long day of hiking ahead of me with more elevation gain than I had been treated to most of my recent hiking stints. I headed south around 7:30AM with roughly 25 miles to Peters Mountain Road. It had been nearly 4 months since I got trapped at the trailhead there. Ah, fond memories indeed. I recall there being campsites a short walk from the trailhead, but, as always, I would be keeping my pace up and my eyes peeled for other options.

It has been revealed that the trail briefly crosses to the far side of Route 443 before re-crossing and heading through a meadow. From there it spends time on 3 parallel mountain ridges. The northernmost is Peters Mountain. To its south is Third Mountain, and then Second Mountain. There is a First Mountain, but the Appalachian Trail doesn’t traverse it. From Second Mountain I could clearly make out Swatara Gap through the trees. Stony Creek Valley sits between Second and Third Mountain and it appears a long gravel road runs for miles along the creek. A sign along the trail stated that the village of Rausch Gap used to occupy the space with about 1,000 people. I couldn’t help but notice how clear Rausch Creek was. I wasn’t sure but there seemed to be water being treated in some manner just north of the bridge over the creek.

Passing through the meadow near Route 443.

Looking at Swatara Gap from Second Mountain.

A bit of info on Rausch Gap beside the AT.

What appears to be some sort of filter or water collection along Rausch Creek.

Crystal clear water under the bridge over Rausch Creek.

The trail heads up Third Mountain, a tree lined ridge without much to see. I did notice a number of trails connecting to the AT. The entire area is quite remote. The long mountain ridges make access tricky, so it makes sense that the section wasn’t as settled as the surrounding areas despite the proximity to Harrisburg.

According to recent reports, by early afternoon I was making my way down to route 325 and up to the third and final mountain ridge, Peters Mountain. Through the trees I could make out a familiar sight to the north of spread out farms. As usual, water was quite scarce up on the mountain ridges. My only option for water near the end of my hike was from the spring at Peters Mountain Shelter. “At” is a rather generous preposition to describe the relative location of the spring to the shelter. It requires a 0.2 mile hike down the steep ridge. A sign posted at the shelter indicates 300 steps are required. I’d put it at closer to 400, none of which were easy.

Down at the spring, movement in the distance caught my attention. I caught something that I was sure was a darker, dulled shade of brown than the white-tailed deer I’d been seeing constantly. I thought for sure it must be a coyote and was glad it had decided to trot off in the opposite direction. Upon closer inspection it did seem to be just another deer, the color was certainly unusual though. I climbed back up the steps to the shelter and collected my pack. Staying at the shelter was enticing, it had a loft and loads of space. I figured I would see what the trail ahead would offer and make a decision.

Looking at Third Mountain from Kinter View.

Looking north from Peters Mountain.

In a recent development, 0.9 miles from the shelter is the Table Rock viewpoint. The large rocks at the crest of the ridge provide an open view across to Third Mountain. However, it looked like the sunset was likely going to be just out of view. Sunrise, however, would be quite clear just to the left hand side of the view. Looking ahead, it seemed like the best I could do, and there seemed to be a spot for a 1 person tent. It was sloped, but I was confident I could orient my tent in such away that I would sleep with the slope running down toward my feet. With the campsite boxes checked, I stashed the 2 liters of water I had collected and headed the last 2 miles south to the Peters Mountain trailhead to connect to the point where I’d ended my southern AT hiking back in July.

With almost no minutes to spare I made it back to table rock to catch the last bits of sunlight hitting Third Mountain. I was exhausted and eager to scarf down my dinner and crawl into my tent. My tent theory was spot on, the slope followed the length of my sleeping pad and didn’t wash out right or left. It is not an easy thing to eye since the inside of my Durston tent runs at a funky diagonal angle relative to the rectangular footprint of the rain fly. I didn’t bother setting an alarm for sunrise. There are about 14 hours between sunset and sunrise. Even if I slept 10 hours I’d be up well before the sun would be making its daily appearance.

The view from Table Rock at sunset.

The view from Table Rock at sunset.

The view from Table Rock at sunset.

Total: 27.6 miles, 54,045 steps.

I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am upcoming to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. Recent findings suggest that what you saw on Rausch Creek was a diversion well to treat acid-mine drainage, which is a huge problem in coal-mining regions. The tainted water is funneled through limestone gravel, which raises the pH enough to give trout a fighting chance of survival.

#90801. Ibex Wool Aire Hoodie Review: A Newly introduced Favorite Piece of Gear After 22,000+ Miles of Hiking

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1237 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Ibex Wool Aire Hoodie Review: A Newly introduced Favorite Piece of Gear After 22,000+ Miles of Hiking

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, over the last handful of years, I have completed thru-hikes all across the country, traversing a wide variety of terrain and weather conditions.
  • I choose to carry as few additional pieces of clothing as possible; my midlayer puffy is one of the most important pieces of gear I have.
  • Recently, though, I have been using a new midlayer that I absolutely love.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, over the last handful of years, I have completed thru-hikes all across the country, traversing a wide variety of terrain and weather conditions. I have consolidated and eliminated pieces of gear from my pack in order to make it as light as possible while still maintaining my desired comforts.

I choose to carry as few additional pieces of clothing as possible; my midlayer puffy is one of the most important pieces of gear I have. When I first got into thru-hiking, I started out with a standard puffy from REI, which was nice and warm but quite heavy and bulky. Later on, I switched to a Montbell 1000-fill puffy, which is incredibly lightweight at roughly 4.5 oz. For the weight and size, I loved this puffy and used it for over 17,000 miles.

Recently, though, I have been using a new midlayer that I absolutely love.

A couple of months ago, I received the Ibex Wool Aire Puffy, which is quite different from any other puffy I’ve used before. The outer shell and lining are 100% nylon, while the insulation is 70% wool and 30% polyester.

The Ibex Wool Air Puffy weighs around 12oz, depending on the size, and packs down quite small. As someone who has primarily prioritized eliminating pack weight wherever possible, I often shied away from heavier pieces of clothing in favor of more bare-bones styles. However, the features of this puffy are what I’ve enjoyed most about it, along with the incredible warmth and comfort it provides.

MSRP: $315 Weight: 12 oz (women’s XS) Materials: 100% nylon shell; 70% wool / 30% polyester insulation Size range: XS – XXL.

Men’s Wool Aire here (our dedicated review of the men’s version is forthcoming).

According to recent reports, I’ve taken the Ibex Wool Aire Puffy out for hundreds of miles along the Appalachian Trail in Pennsylvania, as well as on lesser-known trails such as the Laurel Highlands Hiking Trail and Susquehannock Trail in PA. I’m presently using it on the Arizona Trail as temperatures drop.

Most puffy jackets are insulated with either synthetic polyester fill or natural goose or duck down. The Wool Aire, in contrast, is filled with a 90-gram wool blend. Unlike down, which clumps up and loses loft when wet, this wool insulation maintains its loft even when wet and can be worn while you’re actively hiking. This makes it a good option for hikers who want to hike in their puffy and also want to minimize synthetics in their clothing system.

Sources indicate that wool Insulation: Because this jacket is made primarily of wool and nylon fabrics, it is incredibly soft and feels good even against bare skin. In contrast, traditional puffy jackets often stick and cling to sweaty skin and are much less comfortable when damp or sweaty.

I’ve found this wool material does not wet through the same way that other puffy jackets do when worn during active hiking. The Ibex Wool Air puffy also dries out much quicker than puffies that don’t use wicking fabrics such as wool.

According to recent reports, zipper Pockets: There are two zippable front pockets on the jacket, a feature I really enjoy. When thru-hiking it is great to be able to safely carry a wallet, phone, or a room key around town when running errands. Having pockets that zip shut would make it nice and easy to wear the jacket around and not have to carry a fanny pack.

There is also a large, zippered pocket on the interior of the jacket to allow you to safely store away other vital items that you might need, like a headlamp or charging brick.

Peg Leg in the Ibex Wool Aire Hoodie (second from left).

According to recent reports, comfortable: I find myself excited at the end of the day to put on such a cozy and warm layer. This jacket feels so good on my skin. It provides fantastic insulation for sleeping in colder conditions and is definitely something I wish I had had on the Continental Divide Trail when I was hiking in much more unpredictable conditions.

Ideal fit for thru-hiking: In my opinion, this puffy has the perfect size and fit, and having the hood is a wonderful feature to provide additional warmth and insulation.

Recent findings suggest that dispatch from the AZT: “I’ve been loving the Ibex Wool Aire puffy that I’m using out on a longer thru-hike for the first time. That thing is really cozy but doesn’t get me too sweaty because of the wool. I’m surprised how much I’ve hiked in it on the AZT. I think I’ve done more hiking in a puffy on this trail than any other!” – Peg Leg.

According to recent reports, weight: In my opinion, this jacket is worth the weight. However, if you want the lightest possible puffy, this isn’t it. The Wool Aire weighs somewhere around the middle of the spectrum for puffy jackets that I have seen. Very minimalist designs with limited pockets and no hood can weigh in somewhere around 5oz, whereas more insulated puffy jackets can weigh more than a pound.

Industry observers note that even though it is a little heavier than some other jackets, I think it is well worth the weight. I would much rather carry a few extra ounces and know that at the end of the day I will be incredibly comfortable and warm regardless of the weather conditions.

Shop the Women’s Ibex Wool Aire.

According to recent reports, I’m a thru hiker who has hiked 23,000+ miles in the last few years. In 2025 I became the 1st known woman to hike the “Border to Border” Calendar Year Triple Crown & complete over 10,000 miles of hiking in 1 year. In 2023 I became the 2nd known woman to hike the Eastern Continental Trail from Key West, Florida to Newfoundland Canada. I completed my Double Triple Crown between 2022-2025.

Industry observers note that okay, you’ve accomplished a lot, hiking all over the country. . .I’ve followed most of your posts. Interesting. But now, this piece of gear $315???? Wondering who funds your hikes. . .

Recent findings suggest that the disclaimer at the end clearly states that Peg Leg got this jacket for free. She’s open about having brand deals and gear sponsorships as well as working between hikes. Her funding doesn’t seem to be a mystery.
